cf.title: Row contention in regress/parallel_schedule, adding multi-line test groups

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal, and two reviewers support multi-line groups. Three fixable design points remain. The indentation grammar is not reconciled with Daniel's looser rule or the pending scheduling work (standards-compat-2). The rewritten parallel_schedule exists only on master (maintenance-fit-1). The concurrency output is bundled without a named consumer (maintenance-fit-3). The reviewers already in the thread can settle all three.

brief.title: pg_regress: allow multi-line test groups in schedule files
brief.problem: Every change to parallel_schedule edits long single lines, so unrelated patches conflict and need rebases; the author hit two in one week on another patch. The author also finds long lines hard to read and wants one test per line, so line numbers show group size. The audience is Postgres developers.
brief.proposed_design: pg_regress accepts a group that starts with "test:" and continues on following indented lines until the next unindented line. Blank lines and comments may appear inside a group. Unindented non-"test:" lines and empty groups are errors, and v2 also logs each parallel group's measured average concurrency.
user_visible_surface: Schedule file syntax: "test:" may be followed by tests on indented continuation lines, mixed with tests on the "test:" line.
New pg_regress error messages for unindented lines, naming the line, and for empty test groups.
New pg_regress output line per group: "# effective concurrency 1.46 / 2".
src/test/regress/parallel_schedule rewritten to the multi-line form.
author_claims: Multi-line groups reduce rebase conflicts in parallel_schedule.
One test per line is easier to read and makes test counts visible from line numbers.
Logging effective concurrency is a first step toward faster scheduling; "we can't optimise what we don't measure".
brief.thread_state: Michael Paquier gave a +1 and asked for consistent whitespace; Daniel Gustafsson found that v1 accepted empty groups, which v2 fixes, and mentioned unpublished scheduling work that will also change the syntax. Nobody has reviewed v2.1 yet.
unclear: The patch touches no documentation, and the thread does not say whether schedule syntax is documented anywhere that needs updating.
The thread does not say whether other schedule files, extension schedules or out-of-tree users of pg_regress are checked or converted.
The author says the v2 grammar may not match the implementation, and no tests of the parser are listed.
The effective concurrency output is a separate feature in the same patch, and the thread does not discuss splitting it out.
Nobody has said how this relates to the unpublished scheduling work Daniel mentioned.

objections.title: Indentation-based grammar fixed now, while a known redesign is pending
objections.failure_scenario: Extension authors running pg_regress --schedule adopt indented continuation lines in their own schedule files. The scheduling work in message #4 then needs a different syntax and must either keep the indentation rule forever or break those out-of-tree schedules.
objections.argument: In message #4 Daniel reports unpublished scheduling work that will also change the syntax, and he suggests a whitespace-insensitive rule: any names between ^test: and the next test: or EOF. The v2 grammar instead makes indentation meaningful and makes every unindented line an error. Message #5 sketches a third syntax ("test sequentially:", "test concurrently:") and asks to settle multi-line first. That gives two syntax changes in a row with no agreement on how they fit together.
objections.author_must_show: How does the indentation rule fit with the pending dependency-aware scheduling syntax, and why is it better than Daniel's whitespace-insensitive rule?

critic.reasoning: Message #4 says pending work will change the syntax, and message #5 asks to land multi-line first without saying how the two fit. The thread also gives no reason for making unindented lines an error instead of using Daniel's looser rule.

objections.title: Rewriting parallel_schedule breaks clean backpatching of test additions
objections.failure_scenario: A committer fixes a bug, adds a regression test to parallel_schedule on master and backpatches it to all supported branches. Master uses one test per line and the back branches use long single lines, so the schedule hunk fails to apply on every branch. This repeats for each backpatched schedule change until the last pre-change branch goes out of support.
objections.argument: The patch converts all of src/test/regress/parallel_schedule, and the thread says nothing about the stable branches. The rebase conflicts it removes are between pending master patches. The conflicts it adds fall on committers doing backpatches, for about five years. The thread does not weigh one cost against the other.
objections.author_must_show: Will the parser change be backpatched, or how often do backpatched fixes touch parallel_schedule, and is that cost smaller than the rebase cost saved on master?

critic.reasoning: The patch rewrites parallel_schedule on master only, and the thread does not mention stable branches. Back-patched fixes that add a new test file may be uncommon, but that is the frequency the objection asks the author to show.

objections.title: Concurrency logging is a separate feature bundled with the syntax
objections.failure_scenario: A committer who agrees with the syntax change must also accept a new output line for every parallel group in every regression run, buildfarm log and CI log. If the number turns out noisy or misleading on loaded machines, removing it later means touching the same patch that changed the schedule format.
objections.argument: v2 adds the "effective concurrency" output only as a first step toward faster scheduling, with no consumer yet (message #5). It is unrelated to rebase conflicts and was not requested by either reviewer. As one combined commit, a committer can only take both parts or neither.
objections.author_must_show: Can the concurrency output be split into its own patch, and what decision or tool will use this number?

critic.reasoning: The commit message lists effective concurrency as a separate section of the same patch, and no reviewer asked for it or commented on it. Nothing in the thread discusses splitting it out or names a consumer for the number.

refuted.title: Rewritten parallel_schedule makes back-patched test additions conflict
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer fixes a bug and adds a regression test to a group in parallel_schedule on master, then back-patches to all supported branches. Master has one test per line and the back branches keep long single lines, so the hunk does not apply to any back branch. The committer must rewrite the change by hand for each branch, for about five years.
refuted.argument: The patch rewrites all of src/test/regress/parallel_schedule to the new form, but the parser change exists only on master. Adding a test to an existing group is the most common edit to this file in a bug-fix commit. The patch removes conflicts between master patches and adds conflicts between master and every stable branch. Nothing in messages #1, #3 or #5 weighs this trade.
refuted.author_must_show: Will the parser change be back-patched, or how do committers apply schedule edits to stable branches once master uses the multi-line layout?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1. That one states the same back-patch conflict without the unsupported claim that adding a test to a group is the most common bug-fix edit to this file.

refuted.title: Schedule syntax may change twice in a short time
refuted.failure_scenario: The multi-line form is committed and parallel_schedule, isolation and extension schedules adopt it. The scheduling work Daniel mentioned then lands with its own syntax for dependencies. Developers and out-of-tree pg_regress users rewrite their schedules a second time, and pg_regress keeps parsing three forms.
refuted.argument: Message #4 reports unpublished work that "will also change the syntax". Message #5 then sketches another syntax ("test sequentially:", "test concurrently:") and asks to land the multi-line form first. Nothing in the thread checks that the v2 grammar fits either future design, so pg_regress could end up keeping a grammar it would not have chosen.
refuted.author_must_show: Is the v2 grammar compatible with the dependency syntax in message #5 and with the scheduling work Daniel mentioned, so that schedules converted now do not need another rewrite?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2. This version adds claims the material does not support: that isolation and extension schedules would adopt the form, and that pg_regress would keep three forms.

refuted.title: Effective concurrency output has no stated user beyond the author
refuted.failure_scenario: Every developer running make check gets one more output line per parallel group, about forty lines per run. Nobody has asked for this output. If the unpublished scheduling work Daniel mentioned replaces the group model, the line has to be changed or removed, and any script that reads the output breaks.
refuted.argument: The demand shown in the thread is for multi-line groups only: Michael's +1 in message #2 and Daniel's broader syntax idea in message #4. The concurrency line arrived in v2 (message #5) as a separate feature, justified as "we can't optimise what we don't measure". No reviewer has commented on it. Daniel says in message #4 that other unpublished scheduling work will change the syntax, so a measurement tied to the current group model may not outlive that work.
refuted.author_must_show: Who besides the author will use the per-group concurrency line, and why should it ship in this patch instead of a separate one tied to the scheduling work?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-3, which already asks for a split and a named consumer. The "about forty lines per run" figure and the scripts that would break are not in the material.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: Out-of-tree users of pg_regress write schedule files, and v2 makes every unindented non-"test:" line an error.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-2: Indentation-based grammar fixed now, while a known redesign is pending

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The patch rewrites parallel_schedule on master only, so back-patched schedule edits will not apply to stable branches.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: pg_regress gains a second schedule form and a new output line per parallel group, with another syntax change pending.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Why does v2 make indentation meaningful and unindented lines an error, when message #4 suggests taking any names between one "test:" and the next?
Does the v2 grammar fit the scheduling work mentioned in message #4 and the "test sequentially:" form in message #5, so converted schedules need no second rewrite?
Will the parser change be back-patched, and if not, how do committers apply parallel_schedule edits to stable branches?
Can the effective concurrency output become a separate patch, and which tool or decision will use the number?
Does any schedule file that pg_regress accepts today fail under v2, and is the schedule syntax documented anywhere that needs an update?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows pg_regress and the regression test schedules. Michael Paquier and Daniel Gustafsson both reviewed in the thread, and Daniel has earlier pg_regress work (P2).
committability.liability: The owner signs for the schedule grammar, which out-of-tree schedules may adopt. The owner also signs for hand-edited schedule hunks in back-patches until the last single-line branch leaves support, about five years.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v1.1 the same day as the first review and v2 and v2.1 after Daniel's empty-group report, so the author responds to feedback.

priority.reason: The change helps Postgres developers who edit parallel_schedule and touches only pg_regress.c and the schedule file. Two reviewers are engaged, and the open points are a grammar choice, a back-patch policy and a patch split.

provisional_note: Whether the parser implements the grammar in the commit message could not be checked; the author says they may differ and lists no parser tests. Messages #4 to #6 were judged only through the objections and the brief.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Remove reset of testtablespace from pg_regress on Windows"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Remove reset of testtablespace from pg_regress on Windows"
Reverted commit(s): Remove reset of testtablespace from pg_regress on Windows; Lower privilege level of programs calling regression_main
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 2b2a070, that moved the reset of path
"testtablespace" used by the regression tests as a path for tablespaces
(via --outputdir) from pg_regress to the MSVC script vcregress.pl, as
this broke the behavior added by ce5d342 to be able to safely run the
regression test suite with an administrative Windows account using a
restricted token.

Note that before 2b2a070, the code doing the reset in pg_regress.c
included a comment telling that we had better move that out to a
different place, leading to the mistake done in 2b2a070.  Fix this
comment, and document instead that we had better never remove this code,
for the sake of not breaking again the behavior we expect on Windows.

Thanks to Thomas Munro and Andrew Dunstan for the discussion.

precedents_retrieved.title: TAP format output for pg_regress
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Peter Eisentraut, Tom Lane, Andres Freund
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a --format=tap option to pg_regress so automated runners such as the meson test runner can parse its results, while the traditional format stays the default. It also cuts boilerplate from the default output and adds a --verbose option that restores the current detail.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The CF entry was marked Returned with Feedback after it waited on author input for about two weeks; the author had promised a v6 that the visible messages do not show. Open review points were that the patch hid the parallel group and per-test timing lines, and that keeping two output formats that show the same thing may not be worth it. Andres Freund also argued against keeping the old format just for parity with back branches.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Is it worth maintaining two output formats that display exactly the same thing in slightly different ways?

precedents_retrieved.title: Detect test suite sideeffects in pg_regress
precedents_retrieved.summary: pg_regress records the global objects (roles, tablespaces, subscriptions) before a test suite runs, compares them after, and fails if any were left behind. An earlier version ran a user-given test before and after the suite; after review it was rewritten to query the catalogs through libpq.
precedents_retrieved.objection: When several pg_regress runs share one instance, as the contrib tests do in the meson installcheck CI job, the check sees global objects created by tests running at the same time. pg_regress cannot tell those apart, so the check could only be an opt-in option for the main regression tests. The author and Tom Lane agreed that this was not worth it, and the author withdrew the entry after committing the cleanup patch the check had found.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The reason for the failure is that when running multiple pg_regress in parallel against a single instance it is impossible to avoid global object pollution from other tests concurrently executing.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert the commits related to allowing page lock to conflict among parallel group members.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert the commits related to allowing page lock to conflict among parallel group members.
Reverted commit(s): Allow page lock to conflict among parallel group members.; Add assert to ensure that page locks don't participate in deadlock cycle.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts the work done by commits 3ba59ccc89 and 72e78d831a.
Those commits were incorrect in asserting that we never acquire any other
heavy-weight lock after acquring page lock other than relation extension
lock. We can acquire a lock on catalogs while doing catalog look up after
acquring page lock.

This won't impact any existing feature but we need to think some other way
to achieve this before parallelizing other write operations or even
improving the parallelism in vacuum (like allowing multiple workers
for an index).

precedents_retrieved.title: Move tablespace path re-creation from the makefiles to pg_regress (test for mkdir function in the backend)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a mkdir() SQL function to regress.c, so the backend creates the test tablespace directory instead of pg_regress. It aims to restore installcheck runs where the server user differs from the pg_regress user, which commit 6c788d9 broke.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it because nobody showed a need to act: Christoph Berg had a workaround for the Debian suite, and it was unclear whether a server user different from the pg_regress user should be supported at all. Noah Misch also reported that the patch fails when make check is followed by make installcheck against a server running as another user, because rmtree() cannot remove the server-created directory.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
At the
same time, Christoph has a workaround for the Debian suite, so it does
not seem like there is anything to do now, anyway.

precedents_retrieved.title: Enforce creation of destination folders for source files in pg_regress
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Robert Haas, Stephen Frost, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pg_regress create the sql/ and expected/ output directories when a test suite uses only source files and those directories are missing. Extensions would then no longer need to keep empty sql/ and expected/ directories that hold only a .gitignore ignoring everything.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers saw no clear gain, because .gitignore entries for the generated files are still needed, and keeping them inside the existing directories is better than moving them one level up. Robert Haas asked what is wrong with a .gitignore that ignores everything, and Stephen Frost recommended rejection after his review. The author then noted that three committers were unconvinced and nobody else supported the patch, and agreed to mark it rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I don't see this as an improvement. What's wrong with a .gitignore file ignoring everything?

precedents_retrieved.title: Changing the autovacuum launcher scheduling; oldest table first algorithm
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes how the autovacuum launcher picks a database when one is at risk of wraparound, so that it picks the database holding the oldest table in the cluster. Running autovacuum workers advertise in shared memory the datfrozenxid that each database will have after their work, and the launcher uses this to choose.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stopped applying, and the author did not rebase it after Michael Paquier asked for one. Few reviewers took it up, and the author agreed the design needs to be reconsidered after the discussion. That discussion included Alvaro Herrera's older prioritisation patch and the author's later idea that workers report their progress to the launcher.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I would have suggested to mark the patch as returned with feedback
instead as the thing does not apply for some time now, and the author
has been notified about a rebase.

precedents_retrieved.title: Parallel grouping sets
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add parallel execution of GROUPING SETS queries by splitting aggregation into partial and final stages, first by grouping on the union of all grouping columns in workers and doing the grouping-sets aggregation in the leader. The later version instead performs grouping-sets aggregation in workers, tags each partial tuple with a grouping set ID, and has the leader combine results per grouping set, with refactoring of nodeAgg.c (phase reorganisation, sorting inside the Agg node).
precedents_retrieved.objection: The last patch version received no review and no longer applied to HEAD. A PGCon hallway-track discussion of the approach concluded that nodeAgg.c needs refactoring before it is complicated further, and after an off-list discussion with Melanie, who had picked up the patch, the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There was also considerable discussion in a (virtual) hallway-track session
during PGCon which reviewed the approach (for lack of a better description),
deeming that nodeAgg.c needs a refactoring before complicating it further.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
Reverted commit(s): Optimize order of GROUP BY keys
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit db0d67db2401eb6238ccc04c6407a4fd4f985832 and
several follow-on fixes.  The idea of making a cost-based choice
of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound,
but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't
really have.  For example, relying on procost to distinguish the
relative costs of different sort comparators is pretty pointless
so long as most such comparator functions are labeled with cost 1.0.
Moreover, estimating the number of comparisons done by Quicksort
requires more than just an estimate of the number of distinct values
in the input: you also need some idea of the sizes of the larger
groups, if you want an estimate that's good to better than a factor of
three or so.  That's data that's often unknown or not very reliable.
Worse, to arrive at estimates of the number of calls made to the
lower-order-column comparison functions, the code needs to make
estimates of the numbers of distinct values of multiple columns,
which are necessarily even less trustworthy than per-column stats.
Even if all the inputs are perfectly reliable, the cost algorithm
as-implemented cannot offer useful information about how to order
sorting columns beyond the point at which the average group size
is estimated to drop to 1.

Close inspection of the code added by db0d67db2 shows that there
are also multiple small bugs.  These could have been fixed, but
there's not much point if we don't trust the estimates to be
accurate in-principle.

Finally, the changes in cost_sort's behavior made for very large
changes (often a factor of 2 or so) in the cost estimates for all
sorting operations, not only those for multi-column GROUP BY.
That naturally changes plan choices in many situations, and there's
precious little evidence to show that the changes are for the better.
Given the above doubts about whether the new estimates are really
trustworthy, it's hard to summon much confidence that these changes
are better on the average.

Since we're hard up against the release deadline for v15, let's
revert these changes for now.  We can always try again later.

Note: in v15, I left T_PathKeyInfo in place in nodes.h even though
it's unreferenced.  Removing it would be an ABI break, and it seems
a bit late in the release cycle for that.

precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Stabilize test of BRIN parallel create"
Reverted commit(s): Stabilize test of BRIN parallel create
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 4d916dd876c3. The goal of that commit was to
stabilize a test of parallel BRIN build, but using a TEMPORARY table
disables parallel index builds on that table, making the test useless.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent matches this proposal. [P18] covers multi-line pgbench scripts and records no reason, so nothing carries over. [P2] covers pg_regress output formats, and its doubt about keeping two formats concerns output, not schedule syntax. In message #4 the thread mentions unpublished scheduling work that would also change the syntax, but no earlier rejection of this idea.
Two objections raised. Existing single-line schedules keep working, and the new concurrency line is a TAP comment, so the output contract is not affected.

The proposal changes only the pg_regress schedule file parser, its log output and parallel_schedule. It touches no on-disk format, WAL, replication, catalog, wire protocol or server ABI, so this angle has nothing to object to.

The proposal changes the schedule file syntax of pg_regress and adds a timing line to its output, so it has no privilege or exposure aspect. Schedule files are developer-controlled test inputs. Nothing here touches server privileges, authentication, user data or what an unprivileged database user can see or do.
The objections are about cost and sequencing. The goal itself has support from Michael Paquier and Daniel Gustafsson.

Postgres has no existing way to split one parallel group across lines. Each extra test: line in a schedule file starts a new group that runs after the previous one, so it changes the meaning and cannot replace this. No contrib module or external tool fills the gap, and the schedule format belongs to pg_regress itself, so this cannot live outside core. The effective concurrency line could perhaps be derived from per-test timings, but pg_regress does not print each group's wall time, so I cannot name a working alternative.
Demand for the core change is real: parallel_schedule conflicts affect many patch authors, Michael gave a +1 and Daniel proposed a looser syntax. The only demand gap is the added concurrency output.
